newsitem.title: CANADA: High winds batter dikes in flood-weary Manitoba.
newsitem.headline: High winds batter dikes in flood-weary Manitoba.

text.p: Dikes in Canada's flood-ravaged Red River Valley took a battering from high winds on Monday but withstood the challenge without any major breaches.
Winds gusting up to 30 mph (50 km) were the latest test for flood defences that have so far saved Winnipeg, Manitoba's biggest city with 650,000 people, from serious damage.
The winds created white caps up to two feet (60 cm) high on the so-called "Red Sea," an expanse of floodwater twice the size of Hong Kong that has submerged southern Manitoba.

More than 28,000 Canadians and 50,000 Americans have been forced from their homes by the worst flooding in the area in 145 years. The floods devastated southern Manitoba and North Dakota, causing more than $1 billion in damage.

Emergency officials said they would remain on high alert for days as further winds were forecast. "The 1997 flood is far from over. We have some long tough days and weeks ahead of us," said Winnipeg Mayor Susan Thompson.

On a positive note, officials reported that the main dikes held firm on Monday and water levels dropped one to three inches (2.5 to 7.5 cm) from the previous day. In Winnipeg, the water level fell to about 24.2 feet (7.4 meters) after cresting last Thursday at 24.5 feet (7.5 metres) above winter ice level.
"So far, so good," said Larry Whitney, chief flood engineer for the province. "The crest has passed but the danger has not passed. We're going to remain vigilant."

On Monday Canada and the United States announced they would form a joint commission to study ways to avoid a similar disaster in the future. The Red River swelled to 22 times its normal flow last month as record-breaking winter snow melted.

Although the river has crested throughout Manitoba, the floodwaters were expected to stay high for up to two weeks, straining flood defences, many of them temporary dikes built from sandbags, and waves would only add to the pressure.
"The waves make the water pound against the dikes so we are watching very carefully," said Debbie MacKenzie, a spokeswoman for the provincial emergency management programme.
Emergency crews aided by nearly 9,000 Canadian soldiers were checking dikes every 20 minutes and frantic efforts continued to fortify the flood barriers in vulnerable areas.

In Grande Pointe southeast of Winnipeg, barges ferried sandbags to workers scrambling to save the last 25 homes not underwater. But officials were relieved to find the water level had dropped by about seven inches (18 cms) overnight near the community.
Extra water pumps were rushed to the town of East Saint Paul outside Winnipeg on Monday after a sandbag dike failed.
In Winnipeg the Provencher bridge, one of the main arteries across the Red River, was closed to traffic on Monday because engineers feared it had become unstable.
Nevertheless the city has emerged relatively unscathed from the disaster, with only 26 homes damaged.
In southern Manitoba, some residents have begun returning home after being evacuated last week. About 185 residents of the town of Letellier joined the returnees on Monday.
